name: Modality effect
statement: Words that are heard are recalled better than words that are read, and the advantage sits at the end of the list, over one item on short lists and two or three on longer ones.
meaning: Present a list one word at a time and test recall at once. Recall of the final position is higher when the words were spoken than when they were shown on a screen. The gap is large at the end of the list and absent in the middle. Early positions often run the other way, with silent reading beating listening, which the literature calls the inverse modality effect. The first formal account of the advantage was an echo, a brief store holding sound after the sound has stopped. Pazdera and Kahana call that account influential still, while listing the findings that have forced revisions to it. A second and unrelated claim travels under the same name in education research, that a diagram is learned better with spoken narration than with on-screen text. This entry is about the memory finding, and it keeps the teaching claim separate, because the two rest on different evidence and report different sizes.

origin.who: Bennet B. Murdock Jr and Keith D. Walker
origin.where: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
origin.note: Their free-recall paper is the one the free-recall literature cites for the effect. It was still closed on 21 September 2026 at Elsevier, at OpenAlex and at Unpaywall, so what appears here about it is taken from later papers that describe it. Conrad and Hull had published the same asymmetry for serial recall a year earlier in Psychonomic Science. They tested 20 Naval ratings on seven-digit sequences at two digits a second, and the visual and auditory error curves separated reliably only at the last position, p < .001. Their auditory condition was the participant reading each digit aloud rather than hearing it. Crowder and Morton's precategorical acoustic storage paper, which supplied the explanation the effect carried for a decade, appeared in the same year as Murdock and Walker.

evidence: Roediger and Crowder set out the three findings the sensory-echo account rested on: the auditory advantage for the last few items of a list, the suffix effect, and the partial-report advantage in multichannel listening. Their experiment tested the second. 160 Yale undergraduates heard 16 lists of 12 words at one word a second, with half the lists followed by the spoken word 'Recall' and half by a tone sounded twice in rapid sequence. Averaged over serial positions 7 to 12, the spoken cue cost .10 of the proportion recalled under serial-recall instructions, .09 under free recall, .09 under free position recall, and .04 when subjects were told to recall the last few items first. The authors attribute that .04 to a ceiling effect. The same suffix raised recall of the first three positions under the two order-based instructions, F(1, 32) = 4.09, p < .05. The rough equality across the four instruction types, once allowance was made for ceilings, was the problem the authors named: the conditions imposed different delays between the last word and its recall, and a store they say is usually assumed to last about 2 sec should have produced suffix effects of different sizes. Grenfell-Essam, Ward and Tan then ran the comparison across tasks. Forty participants at Essex in each of two experiments took lists of two to twelve words, split between immediate free recall and immediate serial recall. The auditory advantage appeared in both tasks at every list length except two words. In the second experiment it also failed at a list length of eight under free recall, where the authors write that the analysis just failed to reach significance. On short lists it was large and limited to the final serial position, the shape Conrad and Hull had reported for serial recall. On longer lists it was smaller and spread back over the last two or three positions, the shape reported for free recall. Visual advantages appeared at early positions on the longer lists in both tasks. Comparing the magnitude of performance for the two tasks at matched list lengths and serial positions gave r(44) = 0.858 in the first experiment. It gave 0.709 in the second, where the spoken condition was reading each word aloud rather than listening.

replication.headline: Pazdera and Kahana analysed 1,469 people tested online with presentation modality varied between subjects, and found the auditory advantage at the end of the list and the visual advantage at the start of it in the same data.
replication.detail: Experiment 2 assigned 735 participants to visual presentation and 734 to auditory, with lists of 12 and 24 words at two presentation rates. Those 1,469 are the analysed sample. A further 531 people completed the task and were dropped, 430 of them for using written notes. Mixed effects logistic regressions were fitted to the proportion recalled from the last five and the first three positions, and the fixed effects tested by Type III Wald chi-squared tests. Modality had a main effect on recency performance, chi-square(1) = 114.60, p < .001, and on primacy performance, chi-square(1) = 11.63, p < .001. The second effect ran in the visual direction. Experiment 1 varied modality within subjects across 888 analysed participants, with 212 more excluded, and gave chi-square(1) = 189.68 for recency and 97.54 for primacy, both p < .001. No interaction involving modality reached significance in either experiment, and the closest was modality by presentation rate on recency in Experiment 1, chi-square(1) = 3.62, p = .057. The authors then fitted the Context Maintenance and Retrieval model and reproduced both effects by letting temporal context drift faster and context-to-item associations form more strongly under auditory presentation, with no separate store for recent items. Text and figures were read from the accepted manuscript posted by the Computational Memory Lab, accepted on 4 March 2022, which its own first page says is not the copy of record. The published version is open access at the publisher, which returned a bot challenge rather than the article on 21 September 2026.

study.cite: Pazdera, J. K., & Kahana, M. J. (2023). Modality effects in free recall: A retrieved-context account. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 49(6), 866-888.

limits: The structured effect-size fields are empty because no effect size for the memory version was found in the papers read here. They report proportion recalled by serial position, chi-squares and F ratios. The effect has edges. Grenfell-Essam and colleagues found none at a list length of two words in either experiment, and none at a list length of eight under free recall in the second. Beaman obtained a visual advantage in serial recall by requiring recall of the list in two sections, and describes it, judged list-wide, as equivalent in size to the classical auditory advantage. The education claim is a separate literature with a separate record. Ginns applied meta-analysis to 43 independent effects, 39 of them between-subjects and four within-subjects. The ERIC record of that paper was read and states no effect size, so the figure of d = 0.72 attached to it here is taken from Reinwein's abstract and not from Ginns. Reinwein redid the analysis on 86 independent effects and reports d = 0.38, falling to d = 0.20 after Duval and Tweedie trim and fill for publication bias. This page called Crowder and Morton and Penney paywalled and they are not. Both were downloaded in full from Springer on 21 September 2026 and read, as was Conrad and Hull, which the page had called unread. Murdock and Walker, Gardiner and Gregg, Glenberg, Ginns and Reinwein were still closed at their publishers on that date, with no open copy listed by OpenAlex or Unpaywall. What appears here about them is read from Crossref records, from PubMed abstracts, from the ERIC record, and from the review sections of Pazdera and Kahana and of Roediger and Crowder, and it is attributed in each case. Searches covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, ERIC and web search, and no meta-analysis of the memory version of the effect was located.
misreadings: The echo is the first error. Crowder and Morton proposed a precategorical acoustic store holding sound briefly after it stops, and their 1969 paper puts its persistence at 'at least on the order of a few seconds'. Roediger and Crowder in 1976 record the usual assumption as about 2 sec for ordinary material, and add that there is really no valid evidence on the temporal duration of that storage. Crowder wrote in 1979 that the two-second estimate was 'pure conjecture, and there was then no evidence (nor is there now) to prefer it over some other figure of the same order of magnitude', and that it had become the paper's most frequently cited statement. The evidence went past the number. Huang and Glenberg define a long-term modality effect, an auditory advantage for the last list item that survives a filled retention interval. They report that a redundant auditory suffix produced no reliable reduction in recall of that item, which an echoic account predicts it should. Roediger and Crowder had already found the suffix effect to be about the same size under instructions that changed how long the last items waited before recall. The second error is that the effect needs sound. Pazdera and Kahana's review lists it for vocalised reading, silent mouthing, lip reading, sign language and finger spelling, each with its own citations, none of which were read here. Grenfell-Essam and colleagues obtained the effect in their second experiment with reading aloud as the spoken condition. The third error is direction. Hearing does not beat reading across the board. The advantage sits at the end of the list, and early positions can favour silent reading, which Pazdera and Kahana found in both their experiments and Grenfell-Essam and colleagues found at early positions on longer lists. The fourth error is the name. Education research uses modality effect for the claim that a diagram is learned better with narration than with on-screen text. Ginns's meta-analysis of that claim covered 43 independent effects, Reinwein's covered 86 and roughly halved the estimate, and correcting for publication bias halved it again. Penney's model holds that heard and seen words are processed in separate streams, with heard words automatically encoded in an acoustic code that can be held for some time without deliberate attention. Reinwein argues that the teaching effect cannot rest on that model or on Baddeley's working memory. A page that cites Murdock and Walker in support of a rule about slide design has joined two literatures that do not report the same size of effect.

Still closed at Springer on 21 September 2026; read from its PubMed abstract, which is the source for both its own figures and for the d = 0.72 attributed to Ginns. That abstract miscites Ginns as volume 4 and gives Penney's page range as 398-442, and both are wrong.

Gardiner, J. M., & Gregg, V. H. (1979). When auditory memory is not overwritten. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 18(6), 705-719. Glenberg, A. M. (1984). A retrieval account of the long-term modality effect. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 10(1), 16-31. Still closed at the publisher on 21 September 2026; read from its PubMed abstract, which reports five experiments disconfirming echoic, short-term and long-term storage accounts of the effect.

Campbell, R., & Dodd, B. (1980). Hearing by eye. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 32(1), 85-99. Cited by Pazdera and Kahana for lip-read modality and suffix effects; the PubMed record carries no abstract and the paper was not read.
